analysis.investment_thesis: DIACABS is a legitimate turnaround in India's booming power infra sector, but the market has already priced in years of flawless execution at 75x P/E and 68x EV/EBITDA on ₹34 Cr of freshly recovered profits. With negative equity of -₹714 Cr and a revenue base still at one-third of its 2014 peak, this is paying full price for a company that hasn't yet proven it's rebuilt.
key_strengths: Sector tailwind is real — India's power infrastructure boom (renewables, T&D, data centers) drives structural demand for cables and conductors
Revenue recovery is sharp: ₹0 in 2022 → ₹343 Cr in 2024 → ₹1,115 Cr in 2025 (225% YoY growth), showing the turnaround is gaining traction
Operating margins recovering to 12.92% and OCF turned positive (₹77 Cr in FY25), suggesting the business model is operationally viable again
key_risks: Negative equity of -₹714 Cr with reserves at -₹767 Cr — this company is technically balance-sheet insolvent, and book value is meaningless (P/B = -10.95)
Extreme valuation: 74.9x P/E and 68x EV/EBITDA on ₹34 Cr net profit from a just-recovering base; any earnings stumble will be punished severely
History of catastrophic failure: revenue collapsed from ₹3,153 Cr (2014) to near-zero (2022), with cumulative losses destroying all equity — the same management/sector risks exist
red_flags: Negative shareholders' equity (-₹714 Cr) — company emerged from effective insolvency; promoter holds 84% post-restructuring, near-zero FII/DII
Market cap of ₹7,884 Cr is 7x FY25 revenue and 232x FY25 net profit — priced for a decade of flawless execution
Borrowings rising again: ₹456 Cr (2024) → ₹610 Cr (2025) as capex ramps — leverage risk re-emerges on a fragile balance sheet
Finance costs doubling (₹7 Cr → ₹13 Cr) while profits are only ₹34 Cr — very thin margin of safety on interest coverage
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Lynch loves a good turnaround, but the cardinal rule is "don't overpay for the story." DIACABS checks the sector box — India's power T&D push is real, cables and conductors are in structural demand, and the company's product range (EHV cables, HTLS conductors, transmission towers) positions it squarely in the capex boom. The revenue recovery from ₹0 to ₹1,115 Cr in three years is genuinely impressive. But I'd want to buy the turnaround before Wall Street — or in this case Dalal Street — discovers it. At ₹7,884 Cr market cap, the market has already priced in the next five years of growth.

The balance sheet is the dealbreaker. A PEG of 0.75 (74.9 P/E ÷ ~100% earnings growth) looks cheap on paper, but turnaround earnings growth from a near-zero base is the most unreliable growth you can buy. Negative equity of -₹714 Cr means accumulated losses have wiped out every rupee of capital ever invested. Borrowings are rising again (₹610 Cr vs ₹456 Cr), and with only ₹7 Cr cash, the company has zero buffer. Lynch's rule: avoid companies where the debt burden could sink the ship again. This one nearly drowned twice already.
